title: Torch lands in North Africa

facts.text: In the early morning darkness of 8 November 1942, American and British troops began landing in French North Africa in Operation Torch.
About 107,000 Allied troops took part, landing around Casablanca in French Morocco and at Oran and Algiers in Algeria.

The Western Task Force, about 35,000 American troops under Maj. Gen. George S. Patton with Rear Adm. Henry Kent Hewitt commanding at sea, sailed straight across the Atlantic from Hampton Roads, Virginia, to land at Safi, Fedala, and Mehdia near Port Lyautey.
The Center Task Force landed at Oran and the Eastern Task Force at Algiers; both sailed from Britain.
The defenders were the forces of Vichy France, and nobody knew for certain whether they would fight. They did, hardest of all around Casablanca.
Off Casablanca the unfinished French battleship Jean Bart, with only one working turret, traded fire with the battleship USS Massachusetts, which hit her and jammed the turret that morning.
Patton was aboard the cruiser USS Augusta. The landing boat he meant to take ashore was damaged by the blast of the cruiser's own 8 inch guns, and most of his luggage went overboard.
It was the U.S. Army's first large scale amphibious landing under hostile fire. Landing craft grounded on sandbars nobody had scouted, and vehicles failed in the surf.
Most of the fighting was over within three days. Admiral Francois Darlan ordered French forces to stop resisting at noon on 10 November, and Casablanca surrendered on 11 November.
The campaign cost the United States 556 dead and 837 wounded and Britain 574 dead; more than 1,300 Vichy French troops were killed.
The noon film is from a U.S. Navy newsreel of the landings: shell splashes off the coast, carrier planes taking off, and wrecked ships in Casablanca harbor.
Torch opened the road to Tunisia, where Axis forces in North Africa would surrender in May 1943, and the lessons learned shaped the landings in Italy, France, and the Pacific.

photoNote: American troops on board a landing craft heading for the beaches at Oran, Algeria, November 1942. Royal Navy official photographer, IWM A 12661, Crown copyright expired, public domain (via Wikimedia Commons). Oran, not Casablanca; the place line names Casablanca because the noon film and most of the story are there, so the caption can say the photo shows the Oran landing.
photoCredit: American troops in a landing craft heading for the beaches at Oran, Algeria, November 1942. Imperial War Museum A 12661, public domain.

declassified.fact: Not every American in Torch came by sea. Paratroopers of the 509th Parachute Infantry flew more than 1,600 miles from England to make an airdrop near Oran.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Navy film, WW-II Navy Newsreel #30 ('Anchors Aweigh'), about the North Africa landings. Silent. The file is the stretch from 0:20 to 7:15 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times: 0:00 to 0:40 open sea and fleet; about 0:45 to 1:00 a shell splash erupts beside a ship, the strongest moving opener; 0:55 to 1:30 carrier planes take off and fly past; 2:40 to 3:00 a burning ship trails smoke at sea; 3:20 to 4:10 wrecked and sunk ships in Casablanca harbor and the damaged Jean Bart; 4:25 to 5:20 cargo unloaded on the Casablanca docks; 5:40 to 6:00 rescued survivors wrapped in blankets. Leave out the opening title and globe map (before 0:00) and the paratroop and Tunisia material after 7:15 of the reel.
film.license: U.S. Navy film, U.S. government work, public domain (NARA use status undetermined)
film.date_note: A Navy newsreel about the North Africa landings; individual shots are not dated, so the caption should say Navy film of the Torch landings, not film of 8 November itself.

video.note: U.S. Navy film 428-NPC-44333 (NARA 87706), WW-II Navy Newsreel #30 on the North Africa landings, silent; individual shots are not dated. U.S. government work, public domain. Clip from the research copy footage/1942-11-08-torch-reel.mp4 (0:20 to 7:15 of the NARA reel): 0:41.3 to 0:46.0 shell splashes erupt in the sea; 0:48.5 to 0:51.0 a warship at sea, then a shell burst throws up a column of water; 1:16.0 to 1:20.5 a carrier plane takes off past the camera; 3:25.0 to 3:28.0 smoke pours from a wrecked ship in Casablanca harbor. Converted to square pixels.
video.hook: Nobody knew if the French would fight. They did.
